Jacobus Alting
ya-ko'bus awl'ting
n. (Jacobus Alting, 1618–1679, Hebraist and professor of Oriental languages and theology at Groningen)
Alting, a Frisian and Westphalian family name; Jacobus, the Latin form of Hebrew Ya'aqob, Jacob, a heel-catcher, a supplanter.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jacobus Alting was the son of Heinrich Alting and the grandson of Menso Alting, the third of a line of Reformed divines running from Emden to Heidelberg to Groningen. Born at Heidelberg, he studied there and at Groningen, learned Hebrew in London from the Jewish teacher Jacob Abendana, was ordained in England, and in 1643 was made professor of Hebrew and the Oriental tongues at Groningen, adding the chair of theology in 1667. His whole labour was to read the Old Testament in its own language and grammar. He wrote a Hebrew grammar, a Hebrew-point treatise, a Syriac and a Chaldee grammar, and commentaries which took the plain grammatical sense of the words first and the rabbinical tradition afterward, and only as a witness. That method set him against his Groningen colleague Samuel Maresius, who charged him with Judaizing, with slighting the received Hebrew vowel system, and with Coccejan novelty in the covenants. The quarrel ran for sixteen years, cost both men peace, and was never properly settled; the States of the province at last forbade them to write against each other. Alting's works were gathered after his death in five folio volumes. He stands in the dictionary as a reminder that a Reformed man's first duty to the Old Testament is to construe it, and that a doctrine of Scripture which does not issue in grammar is not yet a doctrine of Scripture.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a professor as one who publicly teaches a science in a college; grammar as the art of speaking or writing a language with propriety; and to study as to apply the mind to books and learning.

expand to see more

PROFESSOR, n. One who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university or college, whose business is to read lectures or instruct students in a particular branch.

GRAMMAR, n. [L. grammatica.] The art of speaking or writing a language with propriety or correctness, according to established usage.

STUDY, v.i. To fix the mind closely upon a subject; to muse; to dwell upon in thought; to apply the mind to books.

TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and of speech; hence, a language; the whole sum of words used by a particular nation.

CONTEND, v.i. To strive in opposition; to struggle in argument; to dispute earnestly.

Modern Corruption

Groningen Hebraist whose grammatical reading of the Old Testament against the rabbinical tradition drew a sixteen-year charge of Judaizing from his own colleague.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is nearer home. Alting's method—construe the Hebrew first, weigh the tradition after—is the method the historical-critical school later claimed as its own invention, and it was neither invented by that school nor owned by it. The difference is not grammar but authority. Alting took the text as the word of God and used grammar to hear it; the later school took grammar as a tool for deciding which parts of the text were the word of God and which were a later hand's. The dictionary keeps the grammar and refuses the authority claim.

The principle to recover is that learning in a minister is not a decoration. “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) is a workman's phrase, and the workman needs tools. Alting's quarrel with Maresius was a real fault on both sides—two orthodox men who could not distinguish a difference of method from a difference of faith, and who spent sixteen years proving it. The province was right to silence them both.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew lashon (H3956), tongue or language; Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight, to divide rightly.

Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut a straight line, to handle rightly; “rightly dividing the word of truth”, 2 Timothy 2:15.

Greek spoudazo (G4704) — to make haste, to be diligent, to study; 2 Timothy 2:15.

Hebrew mephorash (H6567) — made distinct, made plain; “distinctly, and gave the sense”, Nehemiah 8:8.

Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine, to sift, to search; Acts 17:11.

Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding, discernment; “with all thy getting get understanding”, Proverbs 4:7.

Usage

"“a workman that needeth not to be ashamed” (2Ti 2:15) — professor of Hebrew and the Oriental tongues at Groningen from 1643."

"“So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly” (Neh 8:8) — the grammatical sense taken first, the rabbinical tradition weighed after."

"“searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) — five folio volumes gathered after his death in 1679."
